Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated.
This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv.
Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in qubits, which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as superposition—which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.
The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.
Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.
In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)
Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.1
These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classical algorithms, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.
Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum circuits. These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.
We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2).
In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components.

title: How the Claude Code team does code review
summary_raw: Article URL: https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122951 Points: 327 # Comments: 306
fulltext:
Engineering
How the Claude Code team does code review
How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents.
We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?
This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.
We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.
When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.
Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.
Code review does two jobs:
- Find and fix issues before they ship
- Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team
This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which checkâautomated or humanâis the right one to catch it?"
Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.
Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.
We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.
Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.
So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.
A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.
Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can runâlike tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the designâand ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.
Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.
Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."
When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:
- CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.
- REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.
Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?
On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.
When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
summary_raw: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard.
fulltext:
OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts.
The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale.
Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission
In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said. “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.”

title: Bug turns one of the biggest fears about Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses into reality
summary_raw: The bug is fixed, but privacy concerns remain.
fulltext:
Some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people’s conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the prompt phrase (“Hey, Meta”), in a bug that Meta says has been fixed.
This week, some users reported online that their Ray-Ban Metas were recording without their consent. A person going by Kindly-Audience-137 on Reddit, for example, said this happened to them across three Meta Ray-Bans and that they had the “Respond without Hey Meta” setting turned off. The person said the Meta AI app “saves audio recordings and text transcripts of these conversations in my conversation history.”
“I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation. Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant,” the Reddit user said.
Android Authority reported the discussions on Tuesday. Later that day it published a response from Meta that read:
“This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review, and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.”
Although Meta’s brief message suggests that the bug is fixed, the broader privacy problem remains.
Unanswered questions
Meta hasn’t said what caused the Ray-Ban Metas to record people without user consent. Reddit user Kindly-Audience-137 said they “first noticed this behavior after a recent firmware update,” but Meta hasn’t confirmed if a faulty update caused the bug.
We also don’t know how many Meta smart glasses were affected. There are a few reports online, but Android Authority said it was unable to replicate the problem before Meta said it fixed it.
Ars Technica sent Meta a message asking what it’s doing to prevent future bugs like this from happening again and how many devices were affected. We’ll update this article if we hear back.
Even a handful of affected devices is cause for concern, though.
Before reports of this bug, privacy advocates had already expressed widespread concerns about Meta’s smart glasses, as well as those from other vendors. Beyond the fear that naturally accompanies the release of new technology that features a microphone and camera, Meta’s glasses pushed the boundaries of privacy further with their more inconspicuous look, prompting concern about how easy it could be for someone to secretly record another person.

In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts, and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations.
Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks. This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.
The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:
For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.
As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.
To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations.
To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:
- Public Availability. Included benchmarks have at least 25 publicly available tasks. We also include Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, where we have access to held-out benchmark prompts and are therefore able to map them to O*NET tasks.
- Agentic Tasks. Included benchmarks ask models to perform agentic tasks, rather than answering questions or advising the user on how to complete a task.
- Economic Realism. Benchmark tasks resemble tasks which humans (or agents) are frequently asked to do in real-world enterprises. Economically valuable tasks are prioritized over academically complex ones.
- Economic Diversity. We capped the number of included benchmarks per job family, in significant part to account for the massive overrepresentation of software engineering and research tasks in popular benchmarks.
- Balanced Difficulty. Benchmarks are not yet saturated by frontier models.
Following work by Wang et al., we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.
To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al.’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.
A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab.
Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.
We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).
By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.
Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.

title: Desire to Move Permanently to U.S. at New Low
summary_raw: Article URL: https://news.gallup.com/poll/708614/desire-migrate-drops-new-low.aspx Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50120664 Points: 36 # Comments: 11
fulltext:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. remains the most desired destination for people who would like to leave their own countries permanently, but Gallup's latest data show it is less attractive than it once was.
In 2025, 15% of adults worldwide who say they would like to move permanently to another country name the U.S. as their preferred destination, the lowest level recorded in nearly two decades of Gallup research. From 2007 to 2009, 24% of would-be migrants named the U.S. as their top choice, and that figure remained near 20% through 2016. Since 2017, it has been at or below 18%.
The rank order of the countries attracting the most interest from potential migrants has seen little change since Gallup’s first measure. Canada ranks second, as it has for several years, with 9% of potential migrants mentioning the U.S. neighbor. The appeal of these desired destinations did not change in 2025, even as the U.S. became less desirable.
Line charts show trends in the percentage of adults worldwide who would like to move permanently to top destination countries from 2007–2009 to 2025. The United States remains the top destination but declines from 24% to 15%. Canada rises from 7% to 9%. The United Kingdom declines from 7% to 4%. Germany, Australia, Spain, France, Japan, Italy, and Saudi Arabia remain broadly stable around 3% to 5%.
Gallup's latest update on migration desire is based on a question asked almost annually: “Ideally, if you had the opportunity, would you like to move permanently to another country, or would you prefer to continue living in this country?” Those who say they would like to move are then asked to name their preferred destination.
Results for 2025 are based on interviews with over 144,000 adults in 140 countries. The current estimates include data from China for 2023, the last time the question was asked there.
The most recent analysis period coincides with a sharp slowdown in international migration into the U.S., amid changes in immigration policy and declining migration desire in several regions. External data suggest global migration more broadly slowed in 2024 after surging post-pandemic.
Declining Desire to Move to the U.S.
The U.S. became less attractive to adults in several regions in 2025, with statistically significant declines in Latin America and the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia.
Latin America accounts for seven of the 16 countries worldwide where the percentage naming the U.S. as a preferred destination fell by at least 10 points. In the region, the percentage fell from 33% in 2024 to 28% in 2025.
Other Latin American countries that saw double-digit declines include U.S. neighbor Mexico, where the latest 21% who want to move to the U.S. matches the previous low set in 2017 and 2018. In Honduras, desire to migrate to the U.S. dropped 35 percentage points, from 71% to 36%, the largest decline in any country in 2025.
Despite the falling numbers, the U.S. remains by far the most desired destination in Latin America and the Caribbean and in sub-Saharan Africa. The picture varies more in other regions.
In Southeast Asia, Japan leads at 23%, compared with 12% for the U.S. In the Middle East and North Africa, Germany attracts 13% and Saudi Arabia 12% of potential migrants, with the U.S. at 9%. In South Asia, Saudi Arabia and the U.S. are roughly tied, each cited by 7%. Within the European Union, Spain, at 11%, and Switzerland, at 8%, rank ahead of the U.S., at 6%.
Global Desire to Migrate Falls, Shifts
Beyond where people want to go, the data also show a shift in how many want to move at all.
Overall, global desire to migrate declined in 2025 to its lowest level in a decade, driven by sharp drops in regions that have long had the highest migration aspirations, including Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa. After holding at a record-high 16% between 2021 and 2024, global desire dipped in 2025 for the first time in years, falling one point to 15%, a level not seen since 2018.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, 25% of adults say they would like to move permanently to another country, the lowest level in a decade. The decline is particularly notable in this region, where migration desire has fallen steadily after peaking at 34% in 2021-2022.
Multiple countries across the region recorded double-digit declines between 2024 and 2025. In Honduras and El Salvador, the percentage of adults wanting to leave fell sharply last year, from levels above 50% in several prior years to 35% and 25%, respectively.
In sub-Saharan Africa, where migration desire remains the highest globally, 33% say they would like to move permanently, also a decade low. As recently as 2023, that figure stood at 37%, ticking upward from 36% in 2021-2022.
In regions that are typically on the receiving end of migrants, the picture is different. Migration desire in the United States and Canada (20%) and the European Union (21%) remains near record highs.
In the U.S., notably, the heightened desire to move abroad is concentrated among women younger than 45. In 2025, 40% of U.S. women aged 15 to 44 say they would move permanently to another country if they had the opportunity, up from 10% in 2014. The trend first rose sharply in 2016 and continued across multiple years, suggesting a broader shift in outlook rather than a short-term political effect.
Bottom Line
It is important to note that desire to migrate is not the same as intent to move. Not everyone who wants to move can or will do so. The 2025 data show that fewer people worldwide are imagining their futures elsewhere, and the U.S., long the world’s most desired destination, is attracting less of that interest than at any point in nearly two decades.
For years, the dominant story in global migration data was a rising desire to move across nearly every region. The 2025 data suggest that pattern is shifting. The declines are widespread and concentrated in the regions that have historically driven global migration.

Polymarket, the prediction market platform, is paying social media users to quote-retweet content from its branded esports accounts. The program includes over 800 participants, according to posts by a Polymarket representative in an internal Discord, and offers rates ranging from $10 to several hundred per post, paid in crypto.
Paying social media users to engage with content is not illegal, and the Polymarket program has robust guidelines around disclosure and the kinds of quote retweets the company is looking for. But the slight “Paid partnership” tag on X — a common sight on the app, and the only public indication that there’s money changing hands — belies the scale and sophistication of Polymarket’s esports operation, which has more than doubled in size since August. And all the while, in the Discord, Polymarket representatives have repeatedly reminded participants in the program to write posts in a way that should appear “organic,” in what one expert said was an effort to ingratiate the prediction market with esports fans and casual observers.
“Literally this needs to look organic and if your X profile looks like Polymarket billboard that looks absoutely [sic] awful,” wrote one Polymarket rep in the Discord.
Polymarket offers two products: Polymarket Global, which is inaccessible to bettors in the United States, and Polymarket US, which is subject to U.S. regulations. In esports — a growing market for the company — Polymarket offers lines around the outcomes of major events and matches, player statistics, as well as novelty bets, including some relating to the teams that players might transfer to in the off-season.1
The prediction market company’s esports outreach is something of an open secret in the esports world — with an emphasis on “open.” Some social media users have expressed dismay over the increasing prevalence of gambling and betting-adjacent companies in the esports scene, having previously been burnt by “here today, gone tomorrow” attention from deep-pocketed crypto companies and venture capital firms. But while elements of the paid marketing program have previously been reported, little concrete information has been revealed until now about the logistical apparatus behind it, the costs involved, and the Discord server from which the program is run — even as the payments by Polymarket to creators have inspired speculation and debate among esports fans.
Emails to Polymarket’s official press line seeking comment, as well as direct messages to numerous Polymarket representatives from the Discord seeking interviews, went unanswered.

title: What on Earth Is Dekton?
summary_raw: Article URL: https://www.worksinprogress.news/p/porcelain Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118828 Points: 63 # Comments: 19
fulltext:
This is our fifth article from Issue 26, which arrived with print subscribers last week. In it, Charles C Mann explains how he learned to love porcelain.
I am aware that I am a bit of a kitchen equipment nerd, okay? So maybe you don’t have to roll your eyes theatrically like my cousins did when I tell you my wife and I got a swanky induction cooktop that was, well, kind of pricey for a middle-class couple? And maybe you can imagine my irritation when it turned out that the swanky induction cooktop – did I mention it was pricey? – did not include the necessary smooth cooking surface above the induction burners, and that you had to buy the cooking surface separately from a separate company, a fact not exactly advertised on the website, and that the surface could not be tempered glass, which is what I had thought was on top of induction ranges, a sheet of which costs maybe $30 per square foot, but a special, newly created material called Dekton that cost five times as much. ‘What on earth is Dekton?’ I asked the heavens, or at least my wife.
My question turned out to have two answers. The first is that Dekton is an artificial material invented by the Spanish company Cosentino in 2013 that is amazingly heat-, pressure-, scratch-, shatter-, and stain-resistant – a high-tech substance that would have been almost impossible to fashion even thirty years ago. The other answer, equally true, is that Dekton is basically porcelain.
Paradoxically, porcelain is both one of humankind’s oldest high technologies and one of its newest. The earliest proto-porcelain was created more than three thousand years ago, and was, for the time, an astonishing technical feat, as unprecedented as the roughly concurrent development of iron metallurgy. Iron technology had its second flowering in the mid-nineteenth century, when the invention of the Bessemer and Siemens-Martin refining processes allowed manufacturers to produce cheap, high-quality steel. Porcelain is having its resurgence today – indeed, high-tech ceramics are key elements in the ongoing upsurge in materials science, the study of the relationship between a substance’s structure and its physical properties.
Much attention is rightfully focused now on the rise of the digital world and the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence. But that attention sometimes obscures the ongoing, equally important transformation of our physical world, the built environment, by materials science. Unleashing a cataract of innovation so ubiquitous as to be almost invisible, materials science has literally changed the walls around us. Porcelain is a reminder that the drive to create new types of matter has long played a powerful role in human history.
Kaolin
The initial steps toward porcelain occurred when potters in northern China started to tinker with an unusual clay, chalk colored and fine grained, called kaolin. Kaolin was known for its color, useful in paints, coatings, and fillers. Potters learned that subjecting this soft, white, unremarkable-looking mud to extreme temperatures produced startling effects.
Ordinary clay looks like amorphous glop but actually is composed of huge numbers of microscopic crystals. The crystals have an unusual structure: flat plates stacked atop each other like playing cards in a deck, loosely held together by hydroxyl groups (hydrogen and oxygen bound together, or -OH, in chemists’ terms). When clay is cooked in a kiln, the hydroxyl groups vibrate and break free, causing the plates to fall apart and reform into long, needle-shaped crystals that lock together into a sturdy structure. Meanwhile, the free hydroxyls merge, becoming water molecules that steam away in the hot kiln, leaving behind oxygen in the new crystals.
Kaolin clay is abundant in kaolinite, a mineral made of aluminum, silicon, oxygen, and hydrogen – Al2Si2O5(OH)4, with the parentheses meaning that each molecule has four hydroxyl groups. When heated in a kiln, kaolinite also loses its hydroxyls and reorganizes itself into a three-dimensional web of needle-like crystals. But when the temperature rises to about 1,200 degrees centigrade, well above the typical level for earthenware pottery, kaolin does something else. The silicon and oxygen break free, forming silica, which forms a thick liquid glass, filling all the spaces around and inside the web of needles, creating a dense, continuous, translucent matrix – porcelain.
In China, like everywhere else, ceramics had been a foundational industry for millennia. Clay was a primary part of construction (bricks, adobe, wattle-and-daub), cooking (pots, tableware), art (paints as well as sculpture), and even communication – clay tablets were the first surfaces used for writing. But porcelain was a giant leap, a concatenation of multiple innovations.
Ordinary kilns couldn’t reach the temperatures required to fire porcelain, partly because their exhaust vents, located on the ‘roof’, let out the hot air almost as fast as it was created, cooling the kiln. (This is a problem for conventional home fireplaces, which are fun to look at in use but wildly inefficient as a means of heating.) Chinese potters designed downdrafts, which forced the hot air to escape through floor vents, trapping the heat around the pottery. Alarmingly, ordinary kilns would shatter or even melt at such high temperatures. Chinese potters invented new types of heat-resistant brick. And so on.
Alltinktur
When Europeans first saw East Asian porcelain, probably in the thirteenth century, they were astounded. Harder, stronger, finer, smoother, and more lustrous than any other pottery, it became an obsessive object of desire, ‘white gold’ for the Continent’s wealthy and powerful. Enormous sets of gleaming white china became symbols of luxury – the private jets and invite-only clubs of the Renaissance era.
Unhappy about the high prices charged by the merchants who imported porcelain from Asia, European elites spent lavishly on efforts to make their own porcelain – and fail

title: How to Formalize All of Mathematics
summary_raw: Article URL: https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/10/16/how-to-formalize-all-of-mathematics/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118512 Points: 46 # Comments: 42
fulltext:
(This is a guest post, written by Jeremy Avigad, Kevin Buzzard, Johan Commelin, Rémy Degenne, Kim Morrison, Oliver Nash and Adam Topaz.)
Mathematicians’ reactions to last week’s big OpenAI release range from excitement to frustration, but one thing is clear: AI has become remarkably good at proving theorems, both formally and informally. The successes in the formal realm have led AI enthusiasts to declare that now is the time to formalize all of mathematics as a legacy for future generations.
We are sympathetic to this proposal. We recognize the power of new technologies for mathematical reasoning and appreciate what they can contribute to the subject we know and love. We are generally optimistic about the role AI can play, but we are deeply concerned by some recent calls to formalize everything as quickly as possible. If done well, a large-scale, coordinated formalization effort could enormously expand mathematical exploration and discovery. Done poorly, it will be, at best, a waste of resources; more likely, it will do lasting damage.
We prefer to see formalization done well. This post therefore clarifies our concerns, describes some of our experiences with AI and formalization, and offers a positive vision of how we can all work toward a world in which all, or almost all, mathematical definitions, theorems, and proofs are equipped with a formal representation, and in which these artifacts help mathematics flourish.
Just as the role of AI in mathematics is a fraught subject these days, so too is its role in formalization. The range of attitudes among expert formalizers toward AI is as wide as the range of attitudes among mathematicians more broadly. We are aware that some of our closest friends and colleagues, whose opinions we value and respect highly, stand strongly opposed to large-scale formalization using AI. Nothing we say here should be taken as representative of the views of any of the organizations or communities with which we are associated.
The concerns
Let’s start with the observation that a formal artifact is not worth much if nobody uses it. When Math, Inc. tried to hijack a project to formalize Maryna Viazovska’s higher-dimensional sphere-packing results last February, it impressively demonstrated what the technology could do, but beyond that, it contributed nothing to mathematics. The original project team kept preparing a quality formalization of the 8-dimensional result and soon discovered that cleaning up the AI-generated code was more trouble than it was worth; it turned out it was better to throw the code away and do it right, still with ample help from AI.
When Anthropic announced that Claude had formally verified Fermat’s Last Theorem with 13 million lines of code written over 11 days, Kevin Buzzard cheerfully lauded the result while also declaring he had no intention of ending his ongoing formalization of a more modern proof. Once again, although the accomplishment is impressive, this piece of AI-generated code probably has little ongoing value.
What is going on here? The theorems were not seriously in doubt, so the value of the formal artifacts lies solely in what we get beyond mere correctness. We want to formalize everything because we want to use the formalizations to do more mathematics, and to do it better than we could have done without them. We want to think about possible generalizations, explore connections between different branches of mathematics, and consider unexpected applications. We want to refactor and improve our knowledge: part of the joy of manual formalization comes from realizing that we can adjust our concepts to make them more elegant, more efficient, and better suited to our purposes. Knowledge isn’t worth having until it contributes to our understanding; the value of a formalization comes from our ability to use and interact with the data.
When OpenAI announced solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations that blow up in finite time, the natural-language proof was accompanied by a Lean formalization. In contrast to the previous examples, the correctness signal played a key role here: there seems to be little doubt now that the solution is correct, even though the natural-language proof is mostly incomprehensible. OpenAI nonetheless drew the mathematics community’s anger over concerns about how it obtained the result, provenance and credit for ideas, and worries that focusing on correctness alone discouraged the exploration and understanding the Millenium prize was meant to foster. So, even here, the unadorned formal artifact is a mixed blessing. OpenAI’s later dump contains astonishing and important mathematics, and at the same time shows a remarkable disregard for readers and for building understanding (some results have been retracted, many of the informal/formal pairs diverge in subtle or significant ways, and most of the informal writeups are impenetrable).
This explains our concern. If spending millions of dollars to formalize mathematics results in libraries nobody uses, it will be a terrible waste of resources. Worse, the project could disincentivize good research and productive use of AI, disrupt the social norms and practices research depends on, and set the field back decades. A grand failure will make it hard, or even impossible, to recover later. A lousy formalization of existing results is worse than no formalization at all.
The positives
Some of the results from the big labs have been done well: OpenAI’s unit distance conjecture work, and Anthropic’s work on the density of Riemann zeta zeroes stand out. They demonstrated impressive new capabilities, contributed to understanding, and the community subsequently built on their work. These are examples of how the labs can contribute positively and we invite further constructive partnerships between the research community and the labs.
Good formal libraries will enable the positive vision we have for the future of mathematical research. Humans, AIs, and the Lean language work in c

title: RFC8950: Announce IPv4 with an IPv6 next-hop
summary_raw: Article URL: https://anuragbhatia.com/post/2026/06/rfc8950-announce-ipv4-with-ipv6-next-hop/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118267 Points: 44 # Comments: 16
fulltext:
RFC8950: Announce IPv4 with an IPv6 next-hop
For the last few days I have been playing with RFC8950 setup, which allows routing of IPv4 on top of IPv6. While logically it’s quite simple, it has a very powerful application towards making “IPv4 an optional” feature riding on top of an IPv6 network (but without any tunnels!)
Some of the interesting use cases:
- A large network can run IPv6 only everywhere on its core and leave IPv4 only on edge devices. This can work without customers doing any tweaking at their end. They still do things the old way but Backbone can run IPv6 only at its core.
- An IP transit backbone can run IPv6 only while exchanging IPv4 routes with its customers/peers/upstream over IPv6 sessions. So IPv4 as a “feature” stays but the network in itself is IPv6 only without the overhead of IPv4 interface config, BGP session config, firewall config, etc.
- An IXP can offer services without IPv4 essentually by using a (unique) IPv6 at the IX LAN & running route server to exchange both IPv4 & IPv6 routes over the IPv6 only session.
Thus what 464XLAT did to the mobile networks - this has the potential to do that for the backbone networks.
How does it work?
Multi-protocol BGP (MP-BGP) supports announcement of IPv4 routes over IPv6 sessions with IPv4 next-hops and IPv6 routes over IPv4 sessions with IPv6 next-hops. RFC8950 extends this feature for IPv4 to have IPv6 next-hops. So for IPv4 address, next hop is IPv6, IPv6 reach works via usual NDP and IPv4 rides on ethernet frames to the same MAC as discovered by the NDP. Technically RFC8950 only impacts control plane decisions by using IPv6 as the control plane but keeps the data plane as it is. IPv4 stays IPv4 & goes as IPv4 over the wire unlike say some tunnel or 464xLAT etc.
Hardware support
As of now it’s quite widely supported by a lot of routing platforms like Juniper JunOS, Cisco IOS XR, Nokia SR OS, Mikrotik, Huawei, BIRD, FRR etc. So, it is very likely supported if you are running a recent version of the OS.
Demo lab
Here’s a fun lab with two customer routers: C1 & C2 connected via provider routers R1-R2-R3 in Container Lab. All routers here are running open source FRR.
- C1 is IPv6 only on the WAN side facing R1. It originates 10.0.0.0/24 to R1 over an IPv6 session.
- R1 & R2 are IPv6 only with no IPv4 anywhere on their interfaces (but carry IPv4 routes in their table)
- R3 has IPv6 with R2 but just IPv4 only with C2. So C2 is like a typical enterprise user who lacks IPv6 deployment and still wants IPv4 only to work.
- R3 has 100.64.0.0/24 and originates it in the IPv4 table (to IPv6 adjacency - R2)
- C2 sits on 100.64.0.2/30 given by R3 and communicate in IPv4 only.
- C1 and C2 can reach each other over this network with parts being IPv6 only without any tunnel.

title: Bark: The Toll-Free BBS for 90s Teens
summary_raw: Article URL: https://blog.bityard.net/articles/2026/October/bark-the-toll-free-bbs-for-90s-teens Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50117504 Points: 30 # Comments: 9
fulltext:
Topics: Retrocomputing
The other day I was thinking about the first communities I found online and, perhaps tangentially, to what degree they influenced the amount of therapy I now require to function normally as an adult. Our family's second computer came from Sam's Club. It was a 386DX with Windows 3.0 but my inner nerd would have nothing to do with cheerful bit-mapped color schemes, preferring instead to exit to MS-DOS and do all necessary computing and gaming from a command prompt and text-based GUIs. Hardware-wise, it looked and felt cheap. The machine was less reliable than the cardboard box it came in. It was a Packard Bell and if you were to read this paragraph to anyone who was into computers in the 1990's, they will hear that name and then simply close their eyes and nod quietly in sympathetic understanding.
(Nostalgic Modem Noises)
Most importantly, it came with a dial-up modem. My mom's series of reactions when I told her I had plugged our new computer into the telephone line were as follows:
- "Huh, you can do that?"
- "But why would you do that?"
- "WHAT HAVE YOU DONE AND HOW MUCH DO WE OWE?!"
Now in my defense, as a semi-rebellious teenager eager to experience literally anything outside languid rural Midwest life, I often leaned hard into the practice of begging forgiveness in lieu of asking permission. Sometimes I even got away with it.
To give a better idea of the timeline and circumstances, the Internet as we know today it only kind of existed in the early 90's. There was email, there were message boards, file exchange programs, remote login to other systems, real-time chat (IRC) and so on. The web was new and promising and free of ads but not at all the main attraction just yet. And unless you lived in a city or attended a university with a well-funded technology department, the Internet was probably not yet accessible to you. Or for the purposes of this article, me.
But bulletin board systems (BBSes) had been around since at least the early 80's. Maybe earlier, I'm not sure. These were computers connected to phone lines. When you called a number with your computer, the other computer answered, and you could interact with whatever software the sysop (system operator) had set up. Usually these contained at least public and private message boards, but many also had places where you could download and upload files, chat in real time with others (if the BBS had multiple lines), or play games.
How I came upon the early essentials necessary to connect our computer to other computers is a complete mystery to me at this point. I didn't know anyone else with a modem and my school's computer situation was about a decade behind: "computer" classes were really typing classes taught by a cartoon cat named PAWS on Apple IIs. Back at home, at a bare minimum, I would have needed a terminal program to dial up and interact with another computer. So did I have one already or did I grab one off a shareware floppy that came in some magazine? Where did I even find the number of the first BBS (bulletin-board system) to call?
What happened next is easier to remember. I racked up quite the collection of informative text files from that first handful of BBSes I found, which generally included programming guides, hacking e-zines (Phrack!), some anarchy-type content, and rather entertaining but unhinged conspiracy theories. And of course, where to find more BBSes. I also clearly remember downloading as much software as I could get my hands on. Plenty of development tools, different modem terminal programs, and scads of DOS utilities. I learned a lot in a very short amount of time about BBS software, doors, Kermit, X/Y/Zmodem and ZIP files. It took about two hours to download enough data to fill up a 1.44MB floppy disk over a 2400 baud modem. (Eventually I managed to con my mom into buying a 14.4kbps modem a little bit later. I still have no idea how. Maybe because we had a free trial of Prodigy and that needed a faster modem to draw all the fancy vector graphics?)
But that all came to a swift end when my mom got the phone bill at the end of the month. In those days, local calls were free, long distance calls cost money. You paid by the minute and it was not especially cheap. The problem was, we lived in a town so small you could just about trip over it on your way to somewhere interesting, so everything outside a 1.5-mile radius was long distance. I never heard what the monetary damage was, but she did state in no uncertain terms that it would not be allowed to happen again.
1-800-YOU-NERD
(Don't actually call this, I don't know where it goes.)
One of the files I happened to grab was a list of toll-free BBSes. Or as we'd say back before more toll-free codes were added, "1-800 numbers." I didn't know exactly what I would find at these numbers, but that was a big part of the appeal. The first list I downloaded was TB01-94.TXT by Doug Schneider. Here are some others that I have in my collection from around that time frame:
- TB06-96.TXT - Newer version of "The Best 800 List", also in in the wayback machine. (Click on the ZIP, not the TXT.)
- ECBALAM.TXT - "1-800- BBS'S ACROSS THE US" by Bryan Balam - Date Unknown
- BBSWORK3.TXT - "BBS's That Actually Work!" by Kevin Ardoin - August 1994
- BBSWOR41.TXT - "BBS's That Actually Work!" by Kevin Ardoin - December 1994
- TRANSBBS.TXT - "TRANSPORTATION-RELATED ELECTRONIC BULLETIN BOARD SYSTEMS (BBS)"
I have a very clear memory of trying numbers in some semi-random order, crossing off the ones that never answered and highlighting interesting ones to come back to later. I wrote notes next to some. The crossed-off lines outnumbered the highlighted lines 10-to-1 at least. If I ran into a busy signal, it would sometimes be quite a while before I came back to it. It turned out that these toll-free computer systems came and went faster than people could update and pass around the text files. The vast majority of the numbers I called responded with any of:
- Endles

title: The Folders Programming Language
summary_raw: Article URL: https://danieltemkin.com/esolangs/folders Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50114342 Points: 178 # Comments: 31
fulltext:
The Folders Language
Created 2015 | Updated 2026 | One of Forty-Four Esolangs, by the creator of Rivulet and Velato
Where directories are code and drive space is infinite
About
Folders is a non-textual language, where code is expressed in containment and order alone. The names of the folders are ignored, apart from alphabetical ordering. In other words, they are pure ordered trees.
Inspired by the Whitespace language, Folders is devoted to the idea of dematerialized code. It began with the question What is more empty than a file with no visible text? The empty folder is clutter, an appendage with no purpose. In git, it is ignored entirely (for this reason, it is suggested that Folders programs put .gitignore files in their deepest reaches).
Folders began as a Windows language. In Windows, folders are an even more extreme measure of emptiness: they take up no disk space at all. For proof, create 352,449 folders and get properties on it. In this way, Folders offers not only a dematerialized approach to code but also infinite storage capacity. Keep all your data encoded in folder names and never worry about running out of space again.
For those who use other operating systems, the emulator below gives some of the experience of how Folders manages data and code.
The original implementation can be found on github.
Encoding
Each command folder has at least one child folder. The number of subfolders in the first folder (alphabetically) indicates the type of command; any arguments are indicated in a second folder; some commands require a third folder. Expressions are the same: the number of folders in the first sub-folder determine what kind of expression it is. The full Language Spec is below.
Temporary data is stored as folders; unlike Folders code, it is the name of the folder that stores the data.
Folders FS
The Folders interpreter does not create temp files; anything not held immediately in memory is stored as a set of temp folders. Unlike Folders code, the name of the folder stores the data itself. The prefered I/O of Folders is another set of folders. This means you can encode all your data in folders, bypassing the "material realm" of files entirely and giving you infinite disk space (attempt at your own risk). Folders lang for code, Folders FS for data storage.
Visualizations
A Folders program is a nil-terminated nested list. Its simplest form is pure containment and order, like this all-array JSON:
That is also how the JS emulator saves/reads Folders programs.
However, other systems of visualization are possible. Folders programs are content as structure and can be applied to raw data of any type. Here is a Truth Machine as a contour map. The thicker lines are containers, and the order of folders is read starting at the upper left (NW corner) and proceeding counter-clockwise.
Other visualizations might be a family tree (with all single parents), a botanical branching structure (like a splitting stalk of wheat), or the paths through a maze.
The red dots indicate a threshhold from a container to a single child.
Language Spec
The language itself is a very simple imperative language with a short list of semantic rules.
For Commands and Expressions, the number of folders in their first child folder determines their use. Types are used directly.
Commands
| Command | # of Folders | Details | 
|---|---|---|
| if | 0 folders | Second sub-folder holds expression, third holds list of commands | 
| while | 1 folder | Second sub-folder holds expression, third holds list of commands | 
| declare | 2 folders | Second sub-folder holds type, third holds var name (in number of folders) | 
| let | 3 folders | Second holds var name (in number of folders), third holds expression | 
|  | 4 folders | Second sub-folder holds expression | 
| input | 5 folders | Second sub-folder holds var name | 
Expressions
| Type | # of Folders | Details | 
|---|---|---|
| variable | 0 folders | Second sub-folder holds var name | 
| add | 1 folder | Second sub-folder holds first expression to add, third holds second expression | 
| subtract | 2 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to subtract, third holds second expression | 
| multiply | 3 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to multiply, third holds second expression | 
| divide | 4 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to divide, third holds second expression | 
| literal value | 5 folders | Second sub-folder holds the type of the value (e.g. two folders for a string, third holds the value) | 
| equal to | 6 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
| greater than | 7 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
| less than | 8 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
Types
| Type | # of Folders | 
|---|---|
| float | 1 folder | 
| string | 2 folders | 
| char | 3 folders |

FLUX 3 Image Klein
Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.
FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.
The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.
Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights
Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters
In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.
FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.
The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints.
For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch.
On the speed–quality frontier
FLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier.
Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image.
Get started
FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API.
Try it
- BFL API: the distilled model is available as flux-3-image-klein, with prompt upsampling and pixel restoration, which preserves unedited regions of an image exactly. Pricing starts at $0.009 per 1K image.

- Reference inference code, including a Gradio demo for bounding-box control.
- Try it out on Hugging Face Spaces.
- Day-one support in ComfyUI, Hugging Face Diffusers, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang Diffusion and vLLM-Omni.
- LoRA training with Ostris's AI Toolkit and recipes in NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel.
- Trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform, serving through NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, vLLM-Omni and SGLang Diffusion.
- On NVIDIA GB300, the distilled model generates a 1MP image in under 0.6 seconds in NVFP4. Serving a LoRA adds around 5% to generation time.
License
The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API.
Safety
In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here.
FLUX 3 Image Klein is the second open weights release from the FLUX 3 family, following FLUX 3 Action. More will follow.

title: You could have invented transformers from memory
summary_raw: Article URL: https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122878 Points: 271 # Comments: 65
fulltext:
Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.
How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?
In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.
The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity.
We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.
Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory.
An outer product memory store#
The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,
$$W = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i k_i\transpose = V\transpose K$$
where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$.1
To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights.2
Aside: a gradient descent step writes a memory
Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer’s output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, so a step with learning rate $\eta$ is
$$W \leftarrow W - \eta\, \bar y x\transpose.$$
This recurrence is a memory update: it updates the weights with a new memory with key $x$ and value $-\eta\bar y$. For more on this view, see Irie, Csordás & Schmidhuber, who express a linear layer trained by gradient descent as attention over all of its training inputs.
To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:
$$f(x) = V\transpose K x = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,(k_i\transpose x).$$
So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.
Recall picks up interference#
So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?
Let’s assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then
$$f(k_j) = \underbrace{v_j}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq j} v_i\,(k_i\transpose k_j)}_{\text{interference}},$$
meaning we get back the value of the target memory, the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.
If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.
What is the outer-product store’s capacity? Here’s an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference’s squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal’s, and
$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \sim \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k}}.$$
Setting this ratio to 1 gives a capacity of
$$M \approx d_k,$$
once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.
Each bar below is one stored memory’s weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory’s weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we’ll build later in the post.
How do we reduce interference?#
Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall.3 To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to reduce interference.
The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store’s capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.
Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more s

title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
summary_raw: https://words.filippo.io/seeds-solved/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122800 Points: 842 # Comments: 315
fulltext:
Subscribe to the Frontier Red Team newsletter
Get updates on our latest red-teaming research and findings.
Frontier Red Team
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.
We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.
Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.
ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from.
Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.
The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:
“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”
Jerry Solinas, 2015
Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.
Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.
In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!
The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.
This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.
Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.
Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.
The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.

title: C++26: The New Debugging Header

fulltext:
If you’ve ever needed to hit a breakpoint programmatically in C++, you’ve probably written something like this:
1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
9
#if defined(_MSC_VER)
    __debugbreak();
#elif defined(__clang__)
    __builtin_debugtrap();
#elif defined(__GNUC__) && (defined(__i386__) || defined(__x86_64__))
    __asm__ volatile("int3");
#else
    raise(SIGTRAP);
#endif
Every major C++ project reinvents this wheel. Boost.Test has debugger_break(), Catch2 has CATCH_BREAK_INTO_DEBUGGER, Dear ImGui has IM_DEBUG_BREAK() and Unreal has UE_DEBUG_BREAK. The platform knowledge required is arcane but well-known to tooling implementers — it just wasn’t standardized.
C++26 fixes this with P2546R5 and its companion P2810R4 thanks to Rene Ferdinand Rivera Morell. A new <debugging> header provides three functions.
The three functions
1
2
3
4
5
6
7
#include <debugging>
namespace std {
    void breakpoint() noexcept;
    bool is_debugger_present() noexcept;
    void breakpoint_if_debugging() noexcept;
}
All three are noexcept and all three are freestanding. None are constexpr — debugging is a runtime concern.
std::breakpoint()
An unconditional breakpoint. When a debugger is attached, execution halts and control is handed to the debugger. On x86, this typically compiles to a single int3 instruction.
When no debugger is present, the behaviour is implementation-defined — on most platforms the process receives a signal (such as SIGTRAP) and will terminate unless the signal is caught.
std::is_debugger_present()
Returns true if the program is currently being traced by a debugger. The check is performed immediately on each call — the result is not cached because a debugger can attach or detach at any time during execution.
How this works under the hood varies by platform. On Windows, for example, an implementation might call ::IsDebuggerPresent(). On Linux, GCC’s libstdc++ reads /proc/self/status and checks the TracerPid field. The standard doesn’t mandate any particular mechanism — the semantics are implementation-defined, with the intended behaviour described in non-normative notes.
What makes this function interesting is that it’s replaceable, in the same sense as operator new and operator delete. You can define your own version:
1
2
3
bool std::is_debugger_present() noexcept {
    return my_hardware_debug_flag;
}
This was introduced by P2810R4 to solve the freestanding problem: on bare-metal platforms, there may be no OS-level way to detect a debugger. Without replaceability, the function would either have to be excluded from freestanding (forcing #ifdef guards everywhere) or return a useless default. Replaceability lets you wire it to whatever your platform provides.
std::breakpoint_if_debugging()
The convenience function most users will reach for. It’s equivalent to:
1
2
if (std::is_debugger_present())
    std::breakpoint();
When a debugger is attached, you hit a breakpoint. When it’s not, nothing happens. This is the pattern that Catch2, Boost.Test, and every other framework implements manually.
Beyond breakpoints
Having is_debugger_present() as a separate function enables more than just conditional breakpoints. You might use it to:
- Produce extra diagnostic output when debugging
- Disable timeouts that would fire during a stepping session
- Switch to a more debugger-friendly allocator
- Skip optimizations that make debugging harder
The separation of concerns is deliberate — breakpoint() and is_debugger_present() are orthogonal building blocks, and breakpoint_if_debugging() is the convenience composition.
Conclusion
<debugging> is another one of those C++26 additions that makes you wonder why it took this long. The platform knowledge is well-understood, every major project already has its own version, and the API is three functions. Sometimes the most useful standard library additions are the simplest ones.

title: “thegentlemanpervert” producing AI CSAM is a NJ prosecutor, say cops
summary_raw: Discord user flagged AI CSAM, triggering arrest of New Jersey deputy AG.
fulltext:
New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested on “felony charges related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM),” Bucks County Detectives said in a press release Thursday.
In the US, cops have vowed to crack down on AI CSAM since at least 2024, when the Department of Justice made one of the earliest arrests. After charging a Wisconsin man with spreading “thousands of realistic images of prepubescent minors” across Telegram and Instagram, the DOJ clarified to law enforcement that “CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.”
On Thursday, New Jersey officials accused 51-year-old Fitzgerald of using AI to make photos from social media of real minors into sexualized images that he then distributed on social media.
Fitzgerald was charged after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received a tip that a Discord user shared an illicit image in July. Cops then used “digital forensics and subscriber records” linked to the Discord account and “associated Internet protocol addresses” to track the user to Fitzgerald’s home address.
After a search Thursday, cops “recovered prompts and scripts used to create artificially generated child sexual abuse material using an AI program,” the press release said. They also found Discord chat logs where Fitzgerald, under the Discord username “thegentlemanpervert_2160_07833,” allegedly “admitted to making multiple illicit images using artificial intelligence and sharing them with other users.”
